slides.alt: MEDICARE, JANUARY 2022 29 doctor groups quit their contracts early and had their targets reset. Two-thirds ended up with a lower one. Why? Two-thirds: from a check made after the pre-registered analysis, against Medicare's published 2022 targets (slide 18).
slides.narration: In January 2022, twenty-nine groups of doctors and hospitals did something odd. They quit their Medicare contracts early and signed new ones, which reset the targets Medicare uses to decide whether they earn a share of savings. By Medicare's own numbers, checked after the study, two thirds of them ended up with a lower target. A more difficult one. So why do it? I ran a study to find out, and I wrote down the rules before I looked at the data. Here's what I found.

slides.alt: A PRE-REGISTERED STUDY OF PUBLIC MEDICARE DATA Why did some Medicare doctor groups hit "reset" early? And what happens when you write down the rules before you look at the data Samuel Harrold
slides.narration: I'm Samuel Harrold, and this is a pre-registered study of public Medicare data. You don't need any background in healthcare or statistics to follow along.

slides.alt: START WITH A FAMILIAR IDEA Imagine next year's sales target is set from what you sold this year. Have a great year, and next year's target gets harder. Economists call this a ratchet: it only clicks one way.
slides.narration: First, a familiar idea. Imagine your boss sets next year's sales targets from what you sold this year. You crush it, and your reward is a harder target. Do too well today, and tomorrow gets tougher. Economists call this a ratchet, because it only clicks one way. Medicare has its own version of this, and it's the key to the whole puzzle.

slides.alt: THE PROGRAM Medicare pays some doctor groups to save money An accountable care organization (ACO) is a group of doctors and hospitals that agrees to be measured on the total cost of care for its Medicare patients. If costs come in under target, the group keeps part of the savings. 511 doctor groups (ACOs) in the program 12.6M people with Medicare assigned to them Source: CMS Shared Savings Program fast facts, as of January 1, 2026
slides.narration: Here's the program. It's called the Medicare Shared Savings Program, and the groups in it are called ACOs, short for accountable care organizations. That's the one acronym you need. An ACO is just a group of doctors and hospitals. Medicare adds up the total cost of care for each group's patients. If it comes in under a target, the group keeps part of the savings. It's big: five hundred eleven groups, covering about twelve point six million people with Medicare.

slides.alt: A MADE-UP EXAMPLE The deal: beat the target, keep a share Per patient, per year Amount Target (the "benchmark") $11,000 Actual cost of care $10,500 Saved per patient $500 x 15,000 patients $7.5 million At a 50% share $3.75M At a 75% share $5.6M Round numbers for illustration; real targets also adjust for how sick patients are, inflation and caps.
slides.narration: Let's use one made-up example with round numbers. Medicare sets this group's target at eleven thousand dollars per patient per year. The group's patients actually cost ten thousand five hundred. That's five hundred dollars saved per patient, or seven and a half million dollars across fifteen thousand patients. How much does the group keep? On the common track, up to half: about three point seven five million. On the top track, called ENHANCED, seventy-five percent: about five point six million. Same savings, almost two million dollars more. Remember that gap.

slides.alt: PART 1 OF A RESET: YOUR OWN SPENDING The catch: the target resets $11,000 old target $10,500 what patients actually cost $10,500 new target starts here: $500 lower Every few years the target is rebuilt from the group's own recent spending. Beat the target today, and tomorrow's target starts lower.
slides.narration: Now the catch. The target doesn't stay put. When a group signs a new contract, Medicare rebuilds the target, starting from the group's own recent spending. Our group spent ten thousand five hundred, so its new target starts there: five hundred dollars lower. Save money, and your next target gets harder. That's the ratchet. If that were the whole story, no successful group would ever want to reset. But there's a second part.

slides.alt: PART 2 OF A RESET: THE NEIGHBORHOOD The target is nudged toward local costs $10,500 the group's starting point $12,000 similar patients in the region +$525 35% of the $1,500 gap If care in your area costs more than you do, your new target moves part of the way up toward it.
slides.narration: Next, Medicare nudges the target toward what similar patients cost in the group's region. Say comparable patients nearby cost twelve thousand dollars. That's fifteen hundred more than our group spent. The first time, the rules move the target thirty-five percent of the way toward the region. Thirty-five percent of fifteen hundred is five hundred twenty-five dollars. So a group in an expensive area gets a boost. How much room a group has for that boost is what I'll call the regional pull. It's the main thing this study measured.

slides.alt: ADD THE TWO PARTS TOGETHER $10,500 + $525 = $11,025 Almost exactly where it started. The loss from beating your target and the gain from your region can cancel out. Hold that thought.
slides.narration: Let's add the two parts. Start at ten thousand five hundred, from the group's own spending. Add five hundred twenty-five for the region. The new target is eleven thousand and twenty-five dollars. The old one was eleven thousand. Almost exactly where it started. The penalty for saving and the bonus for an expensive area cancel out. I picked these numbers on purpose. Keep this picture in mind, because the real data looked a lot like it.

slides.alt: THE PUZZLE The escape hatch: quit early and sign again Contracts normally last five years. A group could end its contract early and start a new one the next day. That did two things at once: 1. Reset the target sooner A new contract means a new target, built from the two parts we just saw. 2. Unlock the bigger share Under the 2022 rules, it was the only way for most groups to move up to the 75% track mid-contract.
slides.narration: So here's the puzzle. Contracts normally last five years, but a group could quit early and immediately sign a new one. Renewing early did two things at once. First, it reset the target sooner. Second, for groups on the main track, it was the only way to move up to the top track, ENHANCED, before their contract ran out. That's the one that keeps seventy-five percent of savings, though it also means owing back up to seventy-five percent of any losses. Two changes, one decision.

slides.alt: WHO TOOK IT In 2022, 29 groups took the escape hatch Out of 334 groups whose contracts began in mid-2019 or January 2020: 29 renewed early on January 1, 2022 277 stayed in their contracts 28 left the program Source: CMS Shared Savings Program enrollment files
slides.narration: I looked at three hundred thirty-four groups whose contracts started in mid-2019 or January 2020. Twenty-nine renewed early, on January first, 2022. I'll call them early renewers, in orange. Two hundred seventy-seven stayed put: the stayers, in blue. And twenty-eight left the program. So what made those twenty-nine different? One caution: twenty-nine is a small number, and I'll be upfront about what that limits.

slides.alt: TWO SUSPECTS Two possible reasons, tangled together A: A better target Reset because the new target would come out higher than the old one. B: A bigger share Reset because it was the way into the track that keeps 75% of savings. Both came with the same decision, so no test can fully pull them apart.
slides.narration: There are two suspects. Suspect A: a better target. Maybe a reset would have raised their target, giving them more room to earn savings. Suspect B: a bigger share. Maybe they wanted the seventy-five percent track, and renewing early was the only door. The trouble is, both came with the same decision, so no test can fully pull them apart. But one of these suspects doesn't hold up the way you'd expect. Before we get there, here's how I made sure I couldn't fool myself.

slides.alt: BEFORE LOOKING AT ANY RESULTS I wrote down every question, every test, and the exact words I'd use for each possible answer, and posted it publicly. Like calling your shot in pool: which ball, which pocket, before you hit.
slides.narration: Before I looked at a single spending number, I wrote down every question I'd ask, every test I'd run, and the exact words I'd use for each possible result. Then I posted it publicly. It's called pre-registration. Think of calling your shot in pool: eight ball, corner pocket. Why bother? Because these files are public, and if you slice data enough ways, something will look exciting just by chance. Researchers fall into that trap without meaning to. Calling the shot means you can tell a planned test from a lucky find.

slides.alt: HOW YOU CAN CHECK Three locks on the process Public timestamp The plan was registered on OSF, an independent site that records the time itself: October 26, 2026. Locked data The code refused to open any spending or results file until the plan was registered. No override. Practice run Everything was tested first on fake data with known answers planted in it, to prove the code could find them.
slides.narration: And you can check it. The plan was registered on OSF, the Open Science Framework, which stamps the time itself, on October twenty-sixth, 2026. The analysis code refused to open any spending file until that registration existed. And I tested everything first on fake data with known answers planted in it. Reviews of the plan before registration also caught a real flaw: my first main test was quietly just a restatement of past savings. Catching that before the plan was locked, instead of after, is the whole point.

slides.alt: FIRST, A CHECK Can the target be rebuilt? Medicare doesn't publish what a group's target would have been after a reset, so I rebuilt it. I tested the rebuild on 101 groups whose real new targets Medicare did publish, with a pass mark set in advance. 0.94 agreement in ranking groups (1.0 = perfect) Pass mark: at least 0.80 1.6% typical miss on a group's target Pass mark: at most 5%
slides.narration: One more check before the results. Medicare doesn't publish what a group's target would have been after a reset, so I rebuilt it from public files. I tested the rebuild on one hundred one groups where Medicare did publish the answer. It passed the bar I'd set in advance: it ranked groups almost exactly the way Medicare did, and the typical miss was one point six percent.

slides.alt: A 30-SECOND GUIDE How to read the numbers that follow Each result is a best guess plus a range of plausible values. What matters most: does the range include zero? +3.4 range 1.7 to 5.4 Clear difference 0 -0.5 range -2.0 to +0.8 Crosses zero 0
slides.narration: Now, how to read the results. Each one is a best guess, the dot, and a range of plausible values, the bar. Ask one question: does the bar cross zero? Here, the best guess is plus three point four, and the whole bar sits above zero. That's a clear difference. Here, the best guess is minus half a point, and the bar crosses zero. That doesn't prove there's no difference. It means we can't tell it apart from none. You'll see both of these again in a minute.

slides.alt: FINDING 1: THE MAIN QUESTION Early renewers were in places where care costs more +3.4% of target, vs. stayers about $385 per patient per year Range 1.7% to 5.4%; clear of zero The gap between local costs and their target was bigger than for stayers. A reset pulls the target toward local costs, so on this part alone, early renewers had more to gain. Dollar figure at the typical 2021 target of $11,312 per patient. Source: CMS public files; pre-registered analysis.
slides.narration: Finding one, the main question. Were early renewers in places where care costs more than their target? Yes. The gap was bigger than for stayers, by about three point four percent of the target. That's roughly three hundred eighty-five dollars per patient per year. It passed the test I set in advance, and by my own rule it counts as evidence for suspect A, the better target. Case closed? Not quite. That's only one of the two parts.

slides.alt: FINDING 2 But they already beat their targets Share of target saved, 2020 average 6.4% early renewers 4.6% stayers Own spending vs. target, compared with stayers -2.1 points of target; range -3.8 to -0.5 Remember the catch: a reset restarts from your own spending. For strong savers, that part cuts the target.
slides.narration: Finding two. Early renewers were already beating their targets, by more than stayers. In 2020 they saved about six point four percent of their target, against four point six for stayers, and the gap held in 2021 too. That comes straight from Medicare's own reports. And remember the catch: a reset restarts from your own spending. For strong savers, that part cuts the target. So one part helps them more, and the other hurts them more.

slides.alt: FINDING 3 The two parts roughly cancel out Early renewers minus stayers, points of target. Bar = best guess; line = range. Regional part (boost) +1.6 Own spending (catch) -2.1 Total (crosses zero) -0.5 Checked afterward against Medicare's real 2022 targets: early renewers' new targets came in 1.3% below their old ones, on average.
slides.narration: Here's what happens when you put them together. The blue bar is the regional boost. Early renewers stood to gain a little over one and a half points more than stayers. The orange bar is the own-spending catch. They stood to lose about two points more, because they'd been saving more. Add them up, and you get the grey bar: about minus half a point, with a range that crosses zero. The boost and the penalty cancel. It's our eleven thousand and twenty-five example, in real data. After the study, I checked what actually happened, using Medicare's published 2022 targets. Early renewers' new targets came in about one point three percent lower on average, and two thirds of them went down. That check wasn't in the original plan, so I'm labeling it as an add-on. But it agrees. So on average, a reset didn't hand these groups a better target.

slides.alt: FINDING 4 Nearly all of them moved to the bigger share 26 of 27 early renewers on the BASIC track moved up to the 75% track 16 of 27 were already at BASIC's top level, one short step from the 75% track Groups at BASIC's higher levels were much more likely to renew early. With only 24 groups in that model, the exact size is probably overstated; the direction is the finding.
slides.narration: Finding four is about suspect B, the bigger share. Of the twenty-seven early renewers on the main track, twenty-six moved up to the seventy-five percent track. And sixteen of them were already at the main track's top level, one short step away. In a model of who renewed, being at a higher level stood out, along with the regional pull. One caution: that model rests on just twenty-four groups, so trust the direction, not the exact size.

slides.alt: FINDING 5 Spending afterward looked about the same Change in spending growth, 2022-2024, early renewers vs. groups that hadn't yet renewed: -0.4% range -4.0% to +2.5% -4% 0 +2.5% What it rules out A drop of more than about 4%, or a rise of more than about 2.5%. Why it's not "no effect" A trend that began before renewing could hide a smaller effect.
slides.narration: Finding five: did renewing change spending? Compared with groups that hadn't renewed yet, early renewers' spending growth was about the same: minus zero point four percent, with a range from minus four to plus two and a half. So we can rule out a drop bigger than about four percent, or a rise bigger than about two and a half. But I can't call it "no effect." I had only one earlier period to compare trends, during COVID, and a trend that started before renewal could hide a small effect. My plan said not to call it an effect in that case, so I don't.

slides.alt: WHAT IT MEANS What this study can and cannot say Can say Which groups chose to reset early What a reset stood to do to their targets, on average Spending didn't shift by more than a few percent Cannot say That renewing caused anything Which reason was "the" reason What early renewal cost Medicare
slides.narration: So what can this study say? It shows which groups chose to reset, what a reset stood to do to their targets, and that spending didn't shift by more than a few percent. What it can't say: that renewing caused anything, since groups chose for themselves; which suspect was the real reason; or what any of this cost Medicare.

slides.alt: SO WHY DID THEY RESET EARLY? Best reading: they were after the bigger share, not a bigger target. An interpretation, not a tested result. It fits a trade built into the 2022 rules: moving up to the 75% track mid-contract required a reset.
slides.narration: So why did they hit reset? On average, not for a better target. By the later check, their targets mostly went down. But nearly all of them got the bigger share, and many were one step away. For a low-cost group that's already saving, keeping seventy-five percent instead of fifty percent can be worth more than a small drop in the target. That's my reading, not a tested result. But it fits how Medicare wrote the rules: if you wanted the bigger share mid-contract, a reset came with it.

slides.alt: LIMITS The fine print 2022 rules only Rules for 2024 and later soften the hit for past savings. Small numbers 29 early renewers; 24 in the model of who chose. Rebuilt targets Good for group averages, rough for any one group. Smaller groups missing 39 couldn't be measured: Medicare hides tiny counts for privacy. One COVID-era baseline Only one before-period to compare spending trends. Not fully independent Some groups share owners or local markets.
slides.narration: A few limits. The biggest: these are the 2022 rules. For contracts starting in 2024 or later, Medicare gives groups credit for past savings, so the trade-off may look different today. The numbers are small. My rebuilt targets are good for averages, rough for single groups. Thirty-nine smaller groups couldn't be measured, because Medicare hides tiny counts for privacy. And there was only one earlier period, during COVID.

slides.alt: WRAP-UP Three things to remember 1 Groups that reset early were low-cost compared with their areas, and already saving more. 2 A reset didn't raise their targets on average. The 75% share is the likelier draw. 3 Writing the rules first lets you trust a result, even a messy one.
slides.narration: Three things to remember. One: the groups that reset early were low-cost compared with their neighbors, and already saving more. Two: a reset didn't raise their targets on average. The bigger seventy-five percent share is the likelier draw. Three, and this goes far beyond Medicare: write down your rules before you look, and people can trust your answer, even when it's messy.
